[[File:Weizac Plaque.jpg|thumb]]
'''Chaim Leib Pekeris''' ({{Langx|he|חיים לייב פקריס}}; June 15, 1908 – February 24, 1993)<ref name=SSDI>{{cite web|title=Chaim L. Pekeris|url=http://www.americanancestors.org/PageDetail.aspx?recordId=83472721|work=Social Security Death Index|publisher=New England Historic Genealogical Society|accessdate=17 March 2011}}</ref> was an Israeli-American physicist and [[mathematician]]. He made notable contributions to [[geophysics]] and the spectral theory of many-electron atoms, in particular the [[helium atom]]. He was also one of the designers of the first computer in Israel, [[WEIZAC]].

==Biography==
Pekeris was born in [[Alytus]], [[Vilna Governorate]] on June 15, 1908. With the assistance of his uncle, Pekeris and his two brothers emigrated to the [[United States]] around 1925.<ref name="Obit">{{cite news |title=Chaim Pekeris |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-modesto-bee-chaim-l-pekeris-1908-1/131767538/ |work=The Modesto Bee |date=March 6, 1993 |location=Modesto, CA |page=55 |access-date=September 14, 2023 |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}} {{Open access}}</ref> He entered the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] in 1925 graduating in 1929 with a B.Sc. in meteorology. Pekeris also took his graduate studies at MIT, studying under [[Carl-Gustav Rossby]]. In January 1933 he married Lea Kaplan, who was also born in Lithuania. He graduated with his [[Doctor_of_Science#United_States|Sc.D.]] [[doctoral degree]] in 1934.<ref name="Obit"/><ref name=Gilbert>{{cite journal|url=https://www.nap.edu/read/11172/chapter/14|title=Chaim Leib Pekeris (June 15, 1908–February 24, 1993)|first=Freeman|last=Gilbert|year=2004|journal=Biographical Memoirs of the National Academy of Sciences|volume=85|pages=217–228|accessdate=19 September 2019|doi=10.17226/11172|isbn=978-0-309-09183-1|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>[http://www.nap.edu/readingroom.php?book=biomems&page=cpekeris.html BIOGRAPHICAL MEMOIRS]</ref>

In 1934 Pekeris joined the faculty at M.I.T. as an instructor in [[geophysics]] in the department of geology. He became a US citizen in 1938.<ref name=Naturalization>{{cite web|title=U.S. Naturalization Records Indexes, 1794-1995|url=http://search.ancestry.com/cgi-bin/sse.dll?ti=0&indiv=try&db=usnaturalizationindexes&h=338116|work=Index to Naturalization Petitions and Records of the U.S. District Court, 1906-1966, and the U.S. Circuit Court, 1906-1911, for the District of Massachusetts|publisher=National Archives and Records Administration (NARA)|accessdate=25 March 2011}}</ref> Pekeris remained at M.I.T until 1941 when he moved to the Hudson Laboratories of [[Columbia University]] to conduct military research. In 1946 he joined the [[Institute for Advanced Study]].

Pekeris and his wife moved to Israel in 1948,<ref name="Obit"/> where he joined the [[Weizmann Institute]] as head of its department of applied mathematics in 1949.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.ldeo.columbia.edu/vetlesen/recipients/1974/clp_laud.html |title=The Vetlesen Prize |access-date=2011-10-13 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120402200703/http://www.ldeo.columbia.edu/vetlesen/recipients/1974/clp_laud.html |archive-date=2012-04-02 |url-status=dead }}</ref> During the [[1948 Arab–Israeli War]] he was involved in a clandestine program in [[New York State]] developing munitions for the newborn State of Israel.<ref>[https://mizrachi.org/hamizrachi/a-bullet-factory-in-the-catskills/ A Bullet Factory in the Catskills]</ref>

In July 1947, an advisory committee for the Applied Mathematics Department of the Weizmann Institute discussed the plan to build the computer. Among the committee's members were [[Albert Einstein]], who did not find the idea reasonable, and John von Neumann, who supported it. In one conversation, von Neumann was asked: "What will that tiny country do with an electric computer?" He responded: "Don’t worry about that problem. If nobody else uses the computer, Pekeris will use it full time!"<ref>{{Cite book |last=Corry |first=Leo |url=https://www.google.co.il/books/edition/Chaim_L_Pekeris_and_the_Art_of_Applying/AXG7EAAAQBAJ?hl=iw&gbpv=1&pg=PA7&printsec=frontcover |title=Chaim L. Pekeris and the Art of Applying Mathematics with WEIZAC, 1955–1963 |last2=Leviathan |first2=Raya |date=2023-04-24 |publisher=Springer Nature |isbn=978-3-031-27125-0 |language=en}}</ref>

The WEIZAC project was initiated by Pekeris, who wanted it as means to solve [[Laplace]]’s [[Theory of tides|tidal equations]] for the Earth's oceans, and also for the benefit of the entire scientific community of Israel, including the Defense Ministry. WEIZAC's first computation was done in October 1955.<ref>{{cite web |title=Remembering WEIZAC: The Beginning of Computing in Israel |website=American Committee for the Weizmann Institute of Science |date=2013-06-08 |url=https://www.weizmann-usa.org/news-media/in-the-news/remembering-weizac-the-beginning-of-computing-in-israel/ |access-date=2026-07-05}}</ref><ref name=weizac>{{cite web |title=weizac |website=Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science |url=https://www.wisdom.weizmann.ac.il/weizac/weizac.html |access-date=2026-07-05}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Corry |first1=Leo |last2=Leviathan |first2=Raya |title=SpringerBriefs in History of Science and Technology |chapter=Introduction: WEIZAC, Pekeris, and Applied Mathematics |publisher=Springer Nature |date=2023 |url=https://cris.openu.ac.il/en/publications/introduction-weizac-pekeris-and-applied-mathematics/ |access-date=2026-07-05 |page=1–10}}</ref>

Pekeris received the Gold Medal from the Royal Astronomical Society in 1980, and the Israel Prize from the State of Israel in 1981.<ref name=Gilbert /> [[Teddy Kollek]], the mayor of Jerusalem from 1965 to 1993, said in 1990: "I have told you a lot about Chaim Pekeris tonight and there is much more that I could tell, but you will understand that there are reasons that I can’t. Let me simply say that Chaim Pekeris played a most significant role in the establishment of the State of Israel."<ref name=Gilbert /> He died in [[Rehovot]], Israel on February 24, 1993.<ref name="Obit"/><ref name=Gilbert />
